title: What Makes Disaster Films Great
summary: Josh and Chuck explore what defines a disaster film, walking through the genre's characteristics (human-made, natural, extraterrestrial, and transportation disasters; ongoing aftermath; large scale; stereotyped characters and all-star casts) and its history from the 1933 film Deluge through the 1936 San Francisco and 1938 Old Chicago, the 1960s Earth disaster films, the 1970s boom led by Irwin Allen (The Poseidon Adventure, The Towering Inferno, Earthquake, Airport films), its decline with The Swarm and When Time Ran Out, the 1990s resurgence sparked by Outbreak, Twister and Independence Day and the duplicate asteroid and volcano films, and the 2000s and 2010s revival with The Day After Tomorrow, 2012, Contagion, The Impossible and Don't Look Up. They discuss recurring tropes (hero scientists, rival officials, Black characters dying first, women sidelined) and close with listener mail about Morgana the Kissing Bandit.
topics: Black characters dying first in horror and disaster films

segments.title: Opening banter on loving disaster movies
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode and say they enjoy disaster movies, with Josh saying he prefers action movies overall.

segments.title: Defining what counts as a disaster movie
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how hard it is to define the genre, covering disaster types (human-made, pandemics, climate, extraterrestrial, transportation), the requirement that the disaster is ongoing or impending, and scale. They mention Speed, The Birds and Night of the Living Dead as borderline cases.

segments.title: Survival, stereotypes and moral categories
segments.summary: They discuss how survival and death are predictable in disaster films, with stereotyped characters, the hero archetype, and the sidelining of women. They describe characters as good, bad, or redeemable.

segments.title: Black characters and disaster movie tropes
segments.summary: Josh raises the trope of Black characters dying early in horror and disaster films and asks listeners for their views. Chuck notes that Black characters often appear as presidents, such as Morgan Freeman and Danny Glover, and they joke about Freeman's earrings.

segments.title: Everyman heroes and summer popcorn fun
segments.summary: The hosts discuss everyman heroes like the oil rig workers in Armageddon, and say that disaster movies are fun summer popcorn fare rather than great art.

segments.title: Modern variations and serious disaster films
segments.summary: Chuck describes how filmmakers mix big and small disasters, citing Leave the World Behind, and contrasts schlocky films with serious ones like The Impossible, a film about the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.

segments.title: Early history: Deluge, 1930s films and the 1960s Earth disaster films
segments.summary: The hosts trace early disaster films, including Deluge from 1933, San Francisco from 1936, Old Chicago from 1938, and Titanic films. They describe Cold War nuclear anxieties and the early 1960s Earth disaster films such as Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea, The Day the Earth Caught Fire, Panic in Year Zero and The Birds.
topics: Cold War nuclear anxiety in film
Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea
The Day the Earth Caught Fire

segments.title: Night of the Living Dead and Godzilla as disaster or monster films
segments.summary: The hosts debate whether Night of the Living Dead, World War Z and Godzilla Minus One count as disaster films, and Chuck classifies Godzilla Minus One as a monster movie.

segments.title: The Andromeda Strain and animal cruelty in filming
segments.summary: Chuck describes being disturbed by the animal treatment in the film The Andromeda Strain. He says the monkey was suffocated with carbon dioxide and then revived, with the ASPCA present.

segments.title: Airport films and the all-star cast
segments.summary: Airport from 1970 led to three sequels. The hosts say its success, its ensemble cast, and its basis in an Arthur Hailey novel defined the disaster film format. They also mention cameos by stars in later films.

segments.title: Irwin Allen and The Poseidon Adventure
segments.summary: The hosts discuss producer Irwin Allen, called the Master of Disaster, and his hits The Poseidon Adventure and The Towering Inferno. They describe Poseidon's plot and the Gene Hackman character, and discuss Towering Inferno's Paul Newman and Steve McQueen pairing.

segments.title: Earthquake and its unintentionally campy effects
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the 1974 film Earthquake, starring Charlton Heston, and its unintentionally campy scenes, including the elevator scene.

segments.title: Decline of the 1970s boom: The Swarm, When Time Ran Out and Airplane parody
segments.summary: The hosts describe how the 1970s boom faded, with Irwin Allen's The Swarm, Beyond the Poseidon Adventure and When Time Ran Out marking its decline. They note the films became ripe for parody, and that Airplane captured the genre.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: A sponsor break occurs here.

segments.title: 1990s disaster film resurgence: Outbreak, Twister and Independence Day
segments.summary: Josh recalls predicting a revival of disaster films in college. Chuck says the 1990s boom started around Outbreak in 1995, with Twister and Independence Day in 1996 often cited. They discuss the CGI effects that made the revival possible and praise Twister, with Philip Seymour Hoffman's wise-cracking side character.

segments.title: Studio competition, duplicate films and 1990s tropes
segments.summary: The hosts describe how studios raced to release similar films, including Armageddon and Deep Impact, and Dante's Peak and Volcano. They discuss Linda Hamilton's role in Dante's Peak as an example of sexism in the genre, mention smaller 1990s films such as Hard Rain, Firestorm, Tornado and Storm, and describe the hero scientist and rival official tropes.

segments.title: Die Hard, Speed and the everyman hero
segments.summary: The hosts debate whether Die Hard and Speed count as disaster films, with Chuck arguing that the people inside the disaster experience it as one. They describe the everyman hero who uses unexpected skills.

segments.title: Early 2000s revival: The Core, The Day After Tomorrow, 2012 and Contagion
segments.summary: The hosts describe the decline after 9/11, the 2003 film The Core, and The Day After Tomorrow as a bridge to the 2010s revival. They discuss 2012, its Mayan calendar anxiety, and Contagion, which Josh names as his favorite disaster film.

segments.title: Global disasters, Sully, Captain Phillips and modern disaster films
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how 2010s disaster films travel internationally, with worldwide landmarks destroyed and foreign actors cast. They mention Sully, Captain Phillips, San Andreas and Skyscraper, and Chuck argues the genre has not burned out because studios release them more sparingly. They praise Don't Look Up as satire that uses disaster films to critique climate inaction.

segments.title: Viewing recommendations
segments.summary: The hosts say they plan to watch more disaster films, recommending Earthquake, Airport 1975 and The Towering Inferno.

segments.title: Listener mail: Morgana the Kissing Bandit follow-up
segments.summary: A listener named John Ritter writes that his father-in-law knows Morgana the Kissing Bandit, who is alive and retired. The hosts respond warmly.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and give the show's contact information.
